key_facts: Classic peripheral signs of **infective endocarditis**: Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, splinter haemorrhages, petechiae, Roth spots.
**Osler nodes** are **tender** nodules on finger and toe pads; **Janeway lesions** are **painless** macules on palms and soles.
Each sign is now seen in under 10–15% of cases because IE is diagnosed earlier.
Fever + new murmur or IE risk + embolic signs → **same-day hospital assessment**.
**Don't start oral antibiotics before blood cultures**; routine dental prophylaxis is not recommended (NICE CG64).

sections.title: Overview
blocks: Classic peripheral signs of **infective endocarditis (IE)**. They are now uncommon (each is seen in <10–15% of modern IE cases) because IE is diagnosed earlier.

ul: **Osler nodes:** **tender**, pea-sized red-purple nodules on the **pads of fingers and toes** (and thenar/hypothenar eminences), lasting hours to days.
**Janeway lesions:** **painless**, flat or slightly raised haemorrhagic macules on the **palms and soles**.
**Splinter haemorrhages:** thin, longitudinal, red-brown/black lines in the nail bed, running in the direction of nail growth.
**"Splinter haemorrhages mean endocarditis"**: most are from trauma; distal, few and in manual workers is typical.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Skin signs come from **infected emboli and immune complexes** shed from the valve.

mech.t: Bacteria colonise a damaged or prosthetic valve, forming a vegetation.
Fragments lodge in small skin vessels: Janeway lesions, splinters, petechiae.
mech.caption: Fragments of a valve vegetation travel to small vessels in the fingertips and palms.

mech.t: Circulating immune complexes cause vasculitis: Osler nodes, Roth spots.
Emboli also reach brain, kidney and spleen.

ul: **Osler nodes:** traditionally **immunological** (immune-complex vasculitis); histology also shows microemboli. They count as an **immunological phenomenon** in the Duke criteria.
**Janeway lesions:** **septic microemboli** with dermal microabscesses (a **vascular phenomenon**), so organisms may be cultured from them.
**Splinters:** rupture of longitudinally oriented nail-bed capillaries (trauma) or microemboli/vasculitis.

sections.title: Clinical features
blocks: The Osler/Janeway distinction is tender vs painless. Look also for **Roth spots** (retinal haemorrhages with pale centres — fundoscopy), conjunctival petechiae, clubbing (subacute), new murmur, fever, splenomegaly, haematuria, and embolic events (stroke, limb ischaemia).

ul: **Endocarditis:** **2023 Duke–ISCVID / ESC 2023 criteria**: **Major:** typical organisms in ≥2 blood cultures; imaging evidence (echo/PET-CT vegetation, abscess, new valvular regurgitation); **Minor:** predisposition (prosthetic valve, previous IE, IV drug use, congenital heart disease, cardiac devices), **fever ≥38 °C**, **vascular phenomena** (major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial haemorrhage, conjunctival haemorrhages, **Janeway lesions**), **immunological phenomena** (glomerulonephritis, **Osler nodes**, Roth spots, positive rheumatoid factor), microbiological evidence not meeting the major criterion
**Tests (hospital):** ≥3 sets of blood cultures **before antibiotics**, echocardiography (TTE → TOE), FBC, CRP, urinalysis.

blocks: **How many splinters matter?** There is **no validated number**. Splinters are more suspicious when they are **new**, **multiple** (several in one nail or across **several nails** — some texts suggest ≥4), **proximal** (rather than distal — trauma), **painful**, and **accompanied by fever, a murmur or IE risk factors**. Context, not count, makes the diagnosis.

sections.title: Management

ul: **Suspected IE** (fever + new murmur or IE risk + embolic/vascular signs) → **same-day hospital assessment**. **Do not start oral antibiotics** before blood cultures — this sterilises cultures and delays diagnosis (a common primary-care pitfall).

**IE prophylaxis (NICE CG64, updated 2016):** antibiotic prophylaxis for dental/other procedures is **not routinely recommended**. Advise high-risk patients on good **dental hygiene**, to avoid body piercing/tattooing, and on **symptoms to report** (persistent fever, night sweats, weight loss).
**People who inject drugs:** harm reduction (needle-exchange, PWID services), awareness of IE (often right-sided, *S. aureus*).

blocks: Recognition and urgent referral; no antibiotic initiation for suspected IE in primary care; counselling of at-risk patients.

quiz.q: When should you think of Osler nodes, Janeway lesions & splinter haemorrhages?
quiz.a: Tender pulp nodules (Osler), painless palm or sole macules (Janeway) or splinters, especially with fever or a murmur.
Immune-complex vasculitis (Osler) and septic micro-emboli (Janeway) from infected heart valves.

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: Fever + signs = same-day admission for blood cultures before antibiotics and echocardiography (modified Duke criteria).
Endocarditis in injecting drug users, people with prosthetic valves or devices; starting antibiotics before cultures.

quiz.q: Name a red flag that needs escalation.
quiz.a: Fever with a new murmur, splinters or Osler/Janeway lesions: **same-day admission**; do not give antibiotics before blood cultures unless septic.
